newsitem.title: CANADA: Canada's Prairie spring seeding off to good start.
newsitem.headline: Canada's Prairie spring seeding off to good start.

text.p: Seeding of spring crops on Canada's Prairies was more than 45 percent complete this week in very good soil conditions, crop weather experts said.

"We saw good snowfall through the winter. That is very, very useful, especially for spring seeding and topsoil moisture and that's exactly what we've seen this year. The moisture's been good to excessive," CWB weather and crop surveillance director Paul Bullock said in an interview.
All wheat seeded area on the Prairies was forecast to be 28.22 million acres in 1997, Statistics Canada said April 30.
That's down 9.2 percent from 1996's 31.08 million acres.
Canola seeded area, however, was forecast to rise 32 percent to 11.585 million acres from 8.8 million in 1996.

"Dry topsoil conditions haven't been a limiting factor," Bullock said. "Some people won't seed oilseeds into a dry topsoil layer because it doesn't germinate very well. This year they haven't had to worry about it for the most part."
Statistics Canada is due to issue its second seeding intentions estimate at 0730 CDT/1230 GMT June 27.
United Grain Growers Ltd is due to issue its second seeding estimate at 1400 CDT/1900 GMT May 28.

Soil moisture as of Thursday was best in Manitoba where moisture levels of 60 percent of optimum capacity or more was reported but southeast Saskatchewan and south Alberta fell under 60 percent, Environment Canada soil science specialist Rick Raddatz said.

"The only area that's of concern is southern Alberta. It could be 15 to 30 percent drier than we're depicting south of Red Deer," Raddatz said. "That's the only area I'm aware of right now that people are showing some concern on."

Spring seeding of the six major crops which includes wheat, barley, canola, flax, rye and oats, was 45 percent complete by Tuesday with Alberta leading at 75 percent finished, Saskatchewan at 40 percent and Manitoba lagging behind due to spring floods, CWB said.
"It's about average for the Prairies," Bullock said.
Winter precipitation usually provides about one-third of the soil moisture needed to grow a crop, the sources saidid.

"You can store up to six inches worth of precipitation in the ground, so you've got your crop seeded, germinated and half grown but if you don't get a rainfall in the summer, it doesn't matter what sort of snowfall you got in the winter, you can still suffer drought stress in western Canada," Bullock said.
"There's no way around it, if it doesn't rain in the summer you don't get the crop," he added.
